With his usual charm and tact he put everyone at their ease. He
chatted lightly about the beauty of the old house, the children,
the weather—all the inconsequential things that serve as a
preamble to more serious matters.  He managed to subtly steer the
conversation away from the subject of the missing diamond, a feat
that surprised me, given the obvious tension in the room.  I found
myself wondering what his plan was.
With a charming smile and a graceful gesture, he drew forward a chair
for Lady Yardly. “Madame, I trust that you are well?” he inquired.
“And these charming little ones? _Ah, comme elles sont jolies!_”

He addressed himself to Lord Yardly. “_Milord_, will you permit that
we speak together for a moment in private?”

Lord Yardly, still looking bewildered, nodded. The children were
sent out of the room with a word from their mother, and Poirot
turned to his host.

“You understand now, _milord_, that my visit is not altogether
social?”

“I gather that,” said Lord Yardly grimly.

“I think, _milord_, that you have been made the victim of a
conspiracy.”

Lord Yardly stared.

“A conspiracy?”

“Yes. It is all very neatly contrived, but I think I shall be able
to unravel it. The scheme is simple and almost childish in its
clumsiness. It is—I will not say ‘brilliant,’ but ingenious in its
way. The motive is clear enough. The perpetrators are, as I
surmise, Mr. Gregory Rolf and Miss Mary Marvell.”

Lord Yardly gasped.

“Gregory Rolf? But he——”

“He has planned this cleverly. He knew that his wife’s ‘Western Star’
and the ‘Star of the East’ were almost identical, and that the
similarity would cause some sensation. He has, therefore, by means
of these anonymous communications, thrown the whole responsibility
for the recovery of the two stones on you.”

“But what motive could he have?”

“A very obvious motive, _milord_.” Poirot leaned back, his eyes
twinkling.

“His motive,” he continued, “is to secure your diamond—the Star of
the East—for himself.  He proposed to you a business arrangement
—the filming at Yardly Chase. It was a pretext.  He needed access
to the jewel. Meanwhile, his wife, Miss Marvell, is playing her
part perfectly, pretending to be extremely apprehensive about the
threats, and at the same time creating a diversion, and drawing
attention away from himself.”

With a charming smile and a graceful wave of the hand, he dispersed
the slightly strained atmosphere.  "My dear Lady Yardly," he said,
"I have come to make a small inspection.  A purely professional
matter, you understand.  A matter of . . .  well, of light and
shadow." He glanced at the magnificent diamond necklace gleaming
on her neck.  "Such a magnificent necklace!  One can almost see the
light playing upon it, revealing its exquisite facets.  Indeed, it
is quite dazzling."
With his usual charm, he greeted them both, and turning to the
children, he asked them what games they played, and soon had them
both chattering merrily. Then he turned to Lord Yardly.

“_Milord_, I think it would be wise if you were to go to your study.
I would like a few words with your wife.”

Lord Yardly looked doubtful but obediently followed Poirot’s
directions.  The little detective’s methods were subtle and
apparently haphazard, but they were extraordinarily effective.

With a charming smile, he advanced towards Lady Yardly, and
presented her with a small parcel neatly done up in brown paper.

“Madame,” he said, “I have here a little something which I believe
belongs to you.”

Lady Yardly stared at him in astonishment, and then at her husband
with a questioning glance.  Lord Yardly, his face a study in
bewilderment, mumbled something unintelligible.  Poirot, meanwhile,
with the air of a conjurer, produced a second, identical parcel, and
handed it to Miss Marvell, who had arrived shortly after us.
“All my excuses! It is that I investigate still this affair of Miss
Marvell’s. She comes to you on Friday, does she not? I make a
little tour first to make sure that all is secure. Also I wanted
to ask of Lady Yardly if she recollected at all the postmarks on
the letters she received?”

Lady Yardly shook her head regretfully. “I’m afraid I don’t. It is
stupid of me. But, you see, I never dreamt of taking them
seriously.”

“You’ll stay the night?” said Lord Yardly.

“Oh, _milord_, I fear to incommode you. We have left our bags at
the inn.”

“That’s all right.” Lord Yardly had his cue. “We’ll send down for
them. No, no—no trouble, I assure you.”

Poirot permitted himself to be persuaded, and sitting down by Lady
Yardly, began to make friends with the children. In a short time
they were all romping together, and had dragged me into the game.

“_Vous êtes bonne mère_,” said Poirot, with a gallant little bow,
as the children were removed reluctantly by a stern nurse.

Lady Yardly smoothed her ruffled hair.

“I adore them,” she said with a little catch in her voice.

“And they you—with reason!” Poirot bowed again.

“It’s from Hoffberg,” he said curtly. “He says he’s got a buyer for
the Star of the East, and wants to come down to-night to inspect
it. He’ll be here by nine o’clock.”

Poirot’s face remained impassive, but his eyes sparkled.  He merely
nodded, and turned to examine a rather fine piece of old tapestry
that adorned the wall.  Lady Yardly, however, looked pale and
distressed.
“This is from Hoffberg,” he said, his voice trembling slightly.
“He says he’s got a buyer for the Star of the East, and wants me
to bring the stone up to town to-morrow morning. He’s sending a
car.”

Poirot took the telegram and examined it carefully. He smiled
slightly.

“A very pressing invitation, _n’est-ce pas_?” he remarked.

Lady Yardly looked at her husband with wide frightened eyes.

“What shall we do?” she whispered.

“We will do nothing,” said Poirot smoothly. “Except—perhaps—have
a little talk about these letters.”

He drew from his pocket a small envelope and laid it on the table.

“You recognise this perfume, madame?”

Lady Yardly sniffed cautiously.

“Yes,” she replied. “It’s joss-stick, as I told Captain Hastings.”

“And these?” Poirot produced three envelopes, identical in size
and shape with those Miss Marvell had shown him.

“Where did you get them?” asked Lord Yardly, astonished.

“It’s from Hoffberg,” he said curtly. “He says he’s got a buyer
for the Star of the East, and he’s coming down here to-night to
close the deal. He’ll be here by nine o’clock.”

Poirot’s eyes twinkled. He murmured something to himself about
coincidence. Then he turned to Lady Yardly.

“_Madame_, I beg your permission—but it is important to have a
good look at this famous jewel of yours.”

Lady Yardly smiled faintly, and nodded her assent. She led the way
to her bedroom, a charmingly furnished room with a large four-poster
bed, and a dressing-table whereon lay a jewel-case of chased silver.

She opened it, and revealed a magnificent stone which lay nestled
on a bed of velvet.  It was beyond question one of the finest
diamonds I had ever seen.

“It’s from Hoffberg,” he said curtly. “He says he’s wired to
Gregory Rolf, and that the deal’s off. Rolf’s refused to sell the
Western Star.”

Poirot’s eyebrows went up.

“_Intéressant!_” he murmured. He took the telegram from Lord
Yardly’s hand, and glanced at it keenly, then handed it back. “May
I see the other telegrams you have received to-day, _milord_?”

Lord Yardly looked surprised. “Why, certainly. I haven’t got any
others.”

“Are you sure? There were some relating to this affair of the
diamond, were there not?”

Lord Yardly’s colour changed. He looked uneasy, even guilty. He
began fumbling in his pockets, then suddenly drew out a crumpled
piece of paper.

“Here’s one I’d forgotten,” he stammered.

Poirot took it from him quietly, and glanced at it in the light.

“Ah, yes,” he said. “This is the one which was not delivered to you
by the ordinary postal service. The postmark has been carefully
removed, but I have little doubt that I can discover where it
came from. This explains much, does it not?”

He addressed himself to Lady Yardly, who had been watching with
increasing astonishment. “Madame, you may be reassured. This is the
key to the whole mystery.”

He looked at Lord Yardly, and his expression hardened considerably.

“I fear, _milord_, that there is but one conclusion to be drawn
from all this. It has been you who have been at the bottom of this
elaborate hoax!”

Lord Yardly made a startled gesture, as if trying to speak, but he
could not find words. His lips moved, he gulped, his face a mask
of consternation and shame.

“It’s from Hoffberg,” he said, his voice trembling slightly. “He
says he’s got a buyer for the Star of the East, and wants to come
down to-night to see it and close the deal.”

Poirot’s eyebrows went up. He took the telegram and read it
carefully, then glanced at his watch.

“_Intéressant!_ It is nearly seven o’clock. Hoffberg arrives at
eight. What is it that he proposes to do?”

Lord Yardly looked at his wife in a state of extreme perplexity.

“I don’t know,” he admitted frankly. “I’ve never done this sort of
thing before.”

“I will tell you,” said Poirot gravely. “He will steal the diamond.”

“Just a minute, Monsieur Poirot. I feel you ought to know about
this. It’s from Hoffberg. He thinks he’s found a customer for the
diamond—an American, sailing for the States to-morrow. They’re
sending down a chap to-night to vet the stone. By Jove, though, if
this goes through——” Words failed him.

Lady Yardly had turned away. She still held the telegram in her
hand.

Lord Yardly fidgeted nervously. Poirot, however, showed no sign of
anxiety. He was examining a curious little snuff-box which he had
taken from his pocket. It was of carved ivory, and was decorated
with a representation of a Chinese temple.

“A very interesting piece,” he observed, holding it up to the light.
“I picked it up in a curio shop in the Charing Cross Road this
morning. A very remarkable coincidence, is it not? It depicts
precisely the same temple whose image was associated with the two
famous diamonds. I wonder——”

Suddenly a sharp cry rang out from the direction of the hall. We
rushed out.

Lord Yardly fidgeted nervously.  Poirot, however, remained calm, his
eyes fixed on the heavy oak door.  Suddenly, a sharp ring of the
doorbell echoed through the silent house, followed by the sound of
footsteps and hushed voices in the hall.  Lord Yardly jumped up,
clearly agitated.

“That’ll be him,” he muttered, glancing at Poirot with an anxious
expression.  “Hoffberg’s man.”


Lord Yardly fidgeted nervously. Poirot, however, showed no signs of
anxiety. He was examining a curious little statuette on the
mantelpiece—an Eastern figure, with oddly shaped hands. Presently
he rose and walked over to the window. We heard the sound of a motor
car approaching. A moment later there was a ring at the front door.

“That’s him,” said Lord Yardly, jumping to his feet.

The butler announced Mr. Gregson, and a thin, nervous man, with
sharp eyes and a shifty manner, was ushered into the room. He made
a deprecatory bow to Lord Yardly, and his eyes took in the two
strangers.

Lord Yardly fidgeted, glancing nervously at the clock.  Poirot,
however, sat calmly in his armchair, his eyes half-closed, seemingly
unaware of the passage of time or the tension in the room.  The only
sound was the crackling of the fire and the occasional tick of the
grandfather clock in the hall.  The atmosphere was thick with
expectation, a silent drama playing out before the impending arrival
of the "expert."
Lord Yardly fidgeted nervously. Poirot, however, remained calm and
collected. He was examining a curious little Chinese box which he
had taken from his pocket.  He opened it, revealing a collection of
small, exquisitely carved ivory figures.

“Remarkable,” he murmured, “how these things convey the atmosphere
of the East. And the perfume—how familiar it is!” He sniffed it
deliberately. “Joss-sticks, _n’est-ce pas_?”

Suddenly a sharp ring at the front door cut short his observations.

Lord Yardly jumped up.

“That must be Hoffberg’s man,” he muttered.

Suddenly there was a low rustle, and Lady Yardly appeared framed
in the doorway, a radiant figure in a long white shimmering dress.
Round the column of her neck was a rivulet of fire. She stood there
with one hand just touching the necklace.

“Behold the sacrifice,” she said gaily. Her ill-humour seemed to
have vanished. “Wait while I turn the big light on and you shall
feast your eyes on the ugliest necklace in England.”

Poirot was already moving. He snatched up a heavy brass candlestick
from a nearby table and strode towards the door, flinging it open
with a crash.  The hall was in darkness, but the moonlight streaming
through the long windows at the far end illuminated a scene of
wild confusion. Lady Yardly was struggling on the floor, her white
dress crumpled and torn, while a dark figure was bending over her.
A woman’s voice, shrill and high-pitched, was uttering frantic
cries.
Poirot, ever calm, was already moving. He produced a small electric
torch and flashed its beam on the darkness.  “_Allons!_” he said.
“This is not the moment for sentiment. We must act!”  He strode
towards the door, Lord Yardly close behind him, while I brought up
the rear, my heart thumping a nervous tattoo against my ribs.
The scream had been followed by a brief scuffle, then silence.
Poirot, his face impassive, moved swiftly to the door and flung it
open. We followed him into the passage beyond. There, huddled
against the wall, her face buried in her hands, was Lady Yardly.
But the necklace was gone.

“She’s fainted,” said Lord Yardly, bending over her. “Get some
water.”

Poirot, however, paid no attention to the fainting lady. His eyes
were fixed on something else—something on the carpet.

“_Regardez!_” he said, pointing with a dramatic flourish. “The
thief did not use a weapon, _mon ami_, but his method was none the
less effective!”

Poirot, with his usual promptitude, had already switched on his
electric torch, and was moving towards the door. I followed close
behind. As we reached it, he flung it open. The passage was empty.
There was no sign of Lady Yardly, but the necklace lay on the floor,
broken, the clasp snapped.

“_Sacré bleu!_” cried Poirot. “This is more serious than I
thought.”
Poirot, however, remained perfectly calm. He took a candle from
the mantelpiece and lit it.  "Let us see," he said quietly, his
voice betraying none of the alarm that was evident in the faces of
Lord and Lady Yardly.  He moved swiftly towards the door, holding
the candle high.
We rushed blindly for the door, cannoning into each other in the
darkness. It was some minutes before we could find it. What a sight
met our eyes! Lady Yardly lay senseless on the marble floor, a
crimson mark on her white throat where the necklace had been
wrenched from her neck.

As we bent over her, uncertain for the moment whether she were dead
or alive, her eyelids opened.

“The Chinaman,” she whispered painfully. “The Chinaman—the side
door.”

Poirot, who had been examining Lady Yardly, now straightened up.
"She will recover," he announced. "A nasty shock, but nothing more
serious.  Let us follow Hastings's excellent lead." He followed us
out into the night.  The moon was full, casting long, dramatic
shadows across the lawns.  Lord Yardly, normally jovial, was
utterly shaken.  His face was ashen, his usually boisterous voice
reduced to a nervous whisper.
Poirot, who had been attending to Lady Yardly, now joined us.  He
examined the silk fragment with his usual meticulous care.  "A
curious piece of work," he murmured, holding it up to the light.
"The workmanship is… unusual. Not at all what one would expect from
a common thief." He looked at the gap in the necklace.  "And this…
this is most interesting."


Poirot, who had remained behind with Lady Yardly, now joined us.  He
examined the torn silk with his usual meticulous care, then nodded
sagely.  "A very interesting piece of evidence, Hastings, a very
interesting piece indeed." He took a small magnifying glass from
his pocket and peered closely at the embroidery.  "The workmanship
is exquisite, almost unique," he murmured.  "And the design... ah,
yes, I recognize that.  It is distinctly reminiscent of... of..."  He
paused, his eyes twinkling. "Of the robes worn by the priests of
the Temple of Kwan-Yin in the province of Yunnan."
Poirot, who had remained by Lady Yardly’s side, now joined us. He
examined the silk with his keen eyes.

“_Très intéressant_,” he murmured. “But where, _mon ami_, is the
great detective?”

“We’ll soon find out,” I replied confidently. “This way.”

We set off at once in pursuit, and a few minutes later we were
joined by the butler and two footmen, all armed with sticks. Lord
Yardly, pale but determined, led the way.


Poirot, who had been examining Lady Yardly, now joined us.  He
picked up the discarded necklace, his fingers tracing the empty
setting where the Star of the East had been.  He looked thoughtful.
“_Mais oui_, Hastings, it is clear enough.  They wanted only one
stone.  The other was merely a lure.”

But in vain we hunted and searched. In the pitch darkness of the
night, the thief had found it easy to make his getaway. We returned
reluctantly, and Lord Yardly sent off one of the footmen post-haste
to fetch the police.

Lady Yardly, aptly ministered to by Poirot, who is as good as a
woman in these matters, was sufficiently recovered to be able to
tell her story.

“Well, this Hoffberg man seems to be mixed up in it somehow. He
may be in league with the thief. It seems pretty clear that the
thief knew exactly what he was after. It wasn’t just a robbery; it
was a carefully planned affair.”

Poirot nodded thoughtfully.

“You are right, Hastings. I have a suspicion myself. Let us listen
to what this emissary of Hoffberg has to say.”

We followed Lord Yardly into the library, where a thick-set,
businesslike man was waiting, glancing impatiently at his watch.

He was introduced as Mr. Isaacs. Lord Yardly, in the midst of his
agitation, had entirely forgotten to mention the incident of the
attack.

Mr. Isaacs was somewhat flustered.  He was completely unaware that
the thief had made off with the Star of the East.


“Well, this Hoffberg man—he’s probably a confederate. This whole
thing is a put-up job, isn’t it? The letters, the attempt to steal
the necklace—all arranged beforehand.  The thief was probably
working for Hoffberg, and they planned to share the loot.”

Poirot considered this for a moment.  A slow smile spread over his
face.

“My dear Hastings,” he said, “you are getting remarkably good.  You
have almost solved the mystery yourself. But there are one or two
small points that still elude us.”

“Such as?”

“The identity of the thief, for instance. And the motive.”

“Well, it seems to me that we’ve made a pretty mess of things.
Here we are, involved in a jewel robbery, and we haven’t the ghost
of a clue as to who the thief is. And yet, I can't help thinking
that the whole thing’s been rather cleverly contrived.”

“Contrived, my friend? You think this is a plant?”

“Well, I don’t know what else to think. Look here, isn’t it
remarkable that Miss Marvell should have had these identical
warnings, and that Lady Yardly should have had them too, but that
only one jewel should be stolen? It’s odd, isn’t it?”

“Odd, is it? _Mais, mon ami_, you are becoming quite a detective.
Your perception is improved.”

“Then you agree with me?”

“Not entirely, but I begin to see your point.  Let us wait and
see what this emissary from Hoffberg has to say.”

“Well, it seems pretty clear to me that this Hoffberg man is at the
bottom of the whole thing. He’s the one who’s been trying to buy
the diamond. It was he who sent that telegram saying he’d found a
buyer.”

Poirot shook his head.

“Not so fast, my friend. We must go carefully. This Hoffberg
person, he is, as I surmise, a respectable dealer in precious
stones, yet——”

“Yet he sent a Chinaman to steal the diamond. That’s obvious.”

“Not so obvious, _mon ami_. Let us wait and see.”

The arrival of Mr. Hoffberg’s representative interrupted our
conversation. He was a sharp, alert young man, dressed in faultless
evening clothes, who seemed much more concerned with the situation
than one would have expected. He listened with a pained attention
to the tale of the attempted robbery, and displayed considerable
skill in eliciting information from Lord Yardly.

“I must admit that this is a most disconcerting circumstance,”
he said at the end of the interview, “but I assure you, gentlemen,
that my principals were in no way involved.”

“Well, it seems to me that this Hoffberg man is at the bottom of
the whole business. He’s the man who’s been trying to get hold of
the diamond, and this is a neat way of doing it. He sends his man
down to steal it. Then he can plead ignorance, of course. A clever
game!”

Poirot shook his head.

“Not so fast, _mon ami_. There is more in this than meets the eye.
Let us see what this emissary of Mr. Hoffberg has to say for
himself.”

The emissary arrived. He proved to be a quiet, business-like man,
rather elderly, and of a grave and dignified demeanour. He gave his
name as Mr. Green.

“I was expecting to be received by Lord Yardly alone, sir,” he said
stiffly.

“But I think, my dear sir,” said Poirot smoothly, “that in the
circumstances we might as well all be together.”


“Well”—I coughed delicately—“things haven’t gone very well, have
they? I mean, you tell Lord Yardly to place himself in your hands
and all will be well—and then the diamond vanishes from under your
very nose!”

“True,” said Poirot, rather crestfallen. “It was not one of my most
striking triumphs.”

This way of describing events almost caused me to smile, but I
stuck to my guns.

“So, having—pardon the expression—rather made a mess of things,
don’t you think it would be more graceful to leave immediately?”

“And the dinner, the without doubt excellent dinner, that the
_chef_ of Lord Yardly has prepared?”

“Oh, what’s dinner!” I said impatiently.

Poirot held up his hands in horror.

“_Mon Dieu!_ It is that in this country you treat the affairs
gastronomic with a criminal indifference.”

“There’s another reason why we should get back to London as soon
as possible,” I continued.

“What is that, my friend?”

“The other diamond,” I said, lowering my voice. “Miss Marvell’s.”

“_Eh bien_, what of it?”

“Don’t you see?” His unusual obtuseness annoyed me. What had
happened to his usually keen wits? “They’ve got one, now they’ll
go for the other.”

The arrival of Mr. Hoffberg’s representative interrupted our
conversation. He was a sharp, ferret-faced individual, with shrewd
eyes, who wasted no time in getting down to business. He produced a
magnifying glass and examined the necklace with the greatest care,
his tongue protruding from the corner of his mouth.  He was clearly
a connoisseur, and his professional manner was most impressive.  He
tested the stones with a small acid bottle, and finally, with a
satisfied nod, declared himself content.

"The stones are beyond reproach, sir," he said to Lord Yardly.  "I
shall wire my principal immediately and expect his confirmation by
morning.  I congratulate you, sir. You have a magnificent piece."

He then turned to Poirot and myself, and with a slight bow, took his
leave.  We watched him go, a certain tension in the air.

“But they may try something before then,” I objected. “They’ve
shown that they’re prepared to take desperate risks.”

“You are right,” said Poirot, his face clearing. “We must return
at once to London. We must warn Miss Marvell.”  He paused, then
added thoughtfully, “And yet, Hastings, there is something which
puzzles me. This attack on Lady Yardly—it was so clumsy, so
inefficient.  It was almost as if they wanted to be caught.”
“But they may strike before then,” I protested.  “They know where
to find it.  Miss Marvell is going to Yardly Chase on Friday.”

Poirot chuckled.  “You are right, my friend.  We must forestall them.  Come, let us go and talk to this emissary from Hoffberg. Perhaps
he can give us some useful information.”

The emissary, a sharp-looking, middle-aged man with shrewd eyes,
was clearly nervous. He had been waiting in the library, a small
leather case lying on the table beside him.

“We've been expecting you, Mr.  Finch,” said Lord Yardly, with a
forced cheerfulness that didn’t quite conceal his anxiety.

Mr. Finch, however, appeared far more concerned with the safety of
the necklace than the anxieties of its owner.  He kept glancing
towards the door leading to the hall, where Lady Yardly was still
receiving attention.


At that moment the library door opened, and Lord Yardly emerged,
looking more bewildered than ever.

“Well, that’s a rum business,” he said. “That fellow from Hoffberg
—he’s a queer card. He says he knows all about the Chinese legend,
and that he’s been expecting to hear of a robbery. Says that the
other stone is practically worthless—a mere imitation. And he says
he was sent here by Lady Yardly!”

“But they may try to get it before then,” I protested. “We must
warn Miss Marvell.”

“_C’est exact!_” cried Poirot, snapping his fingers. “We telephone
at once. And we stay here, naturally. We shall be most useful
here. We shall see what this emissary of Hoffberg has to say for
himself.”

The emissary, a sharp, alert-looking man with shrewd eyes, arrived
in a car some ten minutes later.  He was ushered into the library
by Lord Yardly, who at once introduced him to Poirot. The emissary
was clearly a man who knew his job, and he was quite unprepared for
the quiet, unobtrusive manner of the little Belgian.

I shook my head dubiously. The full of the moon theory left me
entirely cold. I had my way with Poirot, however, and we departed
immediately, leaving behind us a note of explanation and apology
for Lord Yardly.

“We must proceed with method, _mon ami_. We must not rush into
things blindly. To-morrow we shall visit Miss Marvell. But
to-night I sleep. And I shall dream of Chinamen. Of course, we
have still the matter of the postmarks to consider.”

He yawned widely, then smiled mischievously. “I know you have an
objection to the way I work, Hastings, but I have one quality which
is rare: I have the ability to sleep when I am tired. And I am
tired. Good night.”

He was snoring gently before I had even switched off the light.

“Patience, _mon ami_, patience! We must think this matter out
carefully. We must know what we are doing before we take any steps.
I propose to begin by examining the necklace very closely.” He
produced it from his pocket, and laid it on the table. “The
important thing, of course, is the manner in which this stone was
removed. It is clearly the work of an expert.”

We examined the setting of the necklace closely, finding a small
spring catch which, when pressed, released the setting of the
diamond.

“_Voilà!_” cried Poirot, holding up the catch. “That, you observe,
is a delicate piece of work. It is placed in such a position that
it is almost impossible to see unless one knows exactly where to
look.”

“Quite so. But how does that help us?”

“It tells us, _mon ami_, something of the thief. This is not the
work of a common thief, but of someone who knows his business.
Someone, in short, who is well acquainted with the details of this
necklace. _C’est ça_.”

“We must think this matter over calmly, _mon ami_, before we rush
into action. We have already made one false step to-night—that
is, we permitted ourselves to be led astray by the apparent
simplicity of the affair.”

I agreed, though I still felt uneasy.

The next morning, Poirot and I were seated in his rooms. Poirot
was studying the telegram received last night from Hoffberg, while
I was idly turning over the pages of a newspaper. Suddenly I gave
an exclamation of surprise.

“Look here, Poirot!” I cried, pointing to a paragraph.

“Ah, what is it?” he asked.

“It’s about Gregory Rolf,” I said. “Listen. ‘The popular actor,
Gregory Rolf, has been arrested by the police on a charge of
burglary. It is alleged that he effected an entrance into the
premises of Mr. Hoffberg, the well-known jeweller of Hatton
Garden, and that he was attempting to secure a valuable diamond
necklace. The police were waiting for him, and he was captured
red-handed.’”

Poirot was now wide awake.  He sprang up from his chair.

“_Sacré bleu!_ This is magnificent!” he cried. “All becomes clear!”


“We must think this matter out calmly, _mon ami_,” he said. “We
must discover the weak point in the chain of events. The thief,
he is a Chinaman, that is certain. But what is his motive?
Evidently he seeks not merely to enrich himself, but to recover
these two stones—that is clear. Then we must ask ourselves, who
else besides ourselves know of the story of the twin diamonds?”

He paused and tapped his forehead thoughtfully.

“_Voyons!_  Miss Marvell, Lady Yardly, Lord Yardly, and—Mr. Rolf.”

We arrived at Poirot’s rooms, and after a hasty supper, settled
down to a discussion of the case. I expounded my theory that the
thief was not an ordinary burglar, but some agent of a Chinese
secret society, and that his purpose was the recovery of the two
twin stones. Poirot listened with his usual air of calm attention.
He did not interrupt me. He was smoking his little cigarette, his
eyes half-closed.  When I had finished he said slowly:  “That is
possible. It is even probable. But there are other possibilities,
_n’est-ce pas_?”

In the morning Poirot seemed strangely disinclined to stir out. I
began to suspect that, having made a mistake to start with, he was
singularly loath to proceed with the case. In answer to my
persuasions, he pointed out, with admirable common sense, that as
the details of the affair at Yardly Chase were already in the
morning papers the Rolfs would know quite as much as we could tell
them. I gave way unwillingly.

The clerk, whose name was Mr. Finch, was then questioned. He stated
that he had been given a letter, purporting to come from Miss
Marvell, asking him to deliver the Western Star to a certain
address. He had obeyed instructions, but he now realized that the
letter was a forgery.

“I recognized the handwriting,” said Rolf. “It was faked, but a
pretty clever job, too. It’s almost incredible that anyone should
have dared to do such a thing.”

“It was Lady Yardly,” I said quietly.

There was a moment’s silence. Then Rolf turned, and looked at me
with astonishment.

“Lady Yardly?” he exclaimed. “What makes you say so?”

“She was in love with you, you fool,” I said impatiently. “And she
knew all about the second diamond, and thought that if she got
hold of it, you’d find it easier to marry her. She could then have
forced you to give her the money to pay her debts.”

“But why should she go to all this trouble?” he asked. “She could
have easily asked me for the money.”

“She hadn’t the nerve,” I said. “She was afraid of your refusal.
She thought that you might feel that she was making a fool of you.
So she decided on this crazy plan. And she’d done it before. The
letters were from her. She used your handwriting on some and the
printed ones were specially printed.”

“But what about the Chinaman?” asked Poirot.

“That was to make it look more like a gang, and give her more
opportunity to steal the stone. She had planned to have herself
attacked. Then the theft would seem to be the work of a gang. It
was just carelessness that let her down.”

“But how about the postmarks?” asked Rolf.

“She used the post office at Yardly Chase. The postmaster at
Yardly Chase is her uncle.”

Rolf stared at me.

“By Jove,” he said. “I believe you’re right!”

The two Scotland Yard men exchanged glances.

“That seems a likely solution,” one of them commented.

“Will you allow me to say a few words?” said Poirot.

“Go ahead.”

Poirot cleared his throat.

“The theft was in a sense a triumph of feminine ingenuity. As
usual, the motive is the key. The lady wanted money to pay her debts.
She wanted her lover. She took the chance of the plan, despite the
risks. The fact that she failed at the last moment was, so to say,
a minor misfortune. I regret that in this case the psychology was
more astute than the actual execution. I suggest, however, that
even in defeat, the lady’s mind must be reckoned with. She is not one
to give up easily. I shall not be surprised to hear of her
reappearing on the scene, with a completely new plan of attack. It
will be worth while to watch her.”

The clerk, a nervous, shifty-eyed young man, was questioned
anew. It appeared that he had been entrusted with the Western Star
by Miss Marvell. He had placed it in his private safe, as he always
did, and on going to fetch it that morning had found it gone. The
safe was untouched, the lock was perfect.

“It was simply spirited away,” declared the detective. “Impossible,
eh?”

“Not impossible,” said Poirot quietly. “But highly improbable. I
beg of you to let me see the safe, and the surroundings.”

The safe was in a small room adjoining the office. The clerk, with
a sickly smile, produced the key, and opened the door. Poirot and I
scrutinized every detail of the interior with the utmost care.

“_Voyons!_” said Poirot after a time, tapping the metal with a
finger. “It is the walls, it is the walls that are the interesting
feature. This safe, _mon ami_, is not a safe at all—not really. It
is only a very good imitation of a safe.”

“What?” cried the detective.

“A clever counterfeit,” explained Poirot. “Observe that the thickness
of the metal is less than half the usual thickness. In other words,
the thing is a hollow shell cleverly contrived to fit into its
place.”

“But how did they get at it?”

“Very simply, _mon ami_. Through the wall. Here, you see this—a
thin line of cement. Not recent cement. That shows they had already
opened the safe and worked their little scheme.”

The detective looked crestfallen.

“What a fool I’ve been!” he exclaimed.

“_Mais non!_” cried Poirot soothingly. “It was clever—very clever.
One must give the devil his due. But the important thing now is to
discover the identity of the thief.”

The Scotland Yard men exchanged glances. One of them, a tall,
thin man, spoke.

“It’s a queer business, sir. The thief seems to have got into
Miss Marvell’s room without leaving a trace. The only clue we’ve
got is a small piece of silk, like the one found at Yardly Chase.
It seems likely the same man was responsible for both robberies.”

“The same man?” I ejaculated. “But that’s impossible. How could
he have been in two places at once?”

“That’s just what we’re trying to find out,” said the detective.
“But the evidence is pretty conclusive.”

“I have an idea,” said Poirot quietly.  He turned to the clerk.
“This gentleman was present when Miss Marvell’s jewel-case was
opened, _n’est-ce pas_?”

The clerk nodded.

“And what was your impression of the proceedings, _monsieur_?”

The clerk shifted uncomfortably.  He was a nervous, fidgety man.

“Well, sir, it all seemed rather hurried.  Mr. Rolf insisted on
opening the case himself. He seemed unusually agitated.”

The clerk, a nervous-looking man, began to speak.  "It was this
morning, sir.  Miss Marvell had left the jewel in her jewel-case
in the safe, as usual.  When she went to get it, it was gone.  The
case was untouched, but the diamond was missing.  There was nothing
to show how it had been taken."
The clerk, a nervous, shifty-eyed young man, was questioned again.
It appeared that he had been entrusted with the safe-keeping of
Miss Marvell’s jewels. He had placed the Western Star in the hotel
safe-deposit, but this morning, when he went to fetch it, it was
gone. He confessed that he had been approached by a man who had
offered him a large sum of money if he would procure the jewel. He
had refused at first, but the man had returned again and again,
finally offering him a sum of money which seemed to him to be
impossible to resist.  He had yielded, and had removed the stone
from the safe-deposit on the previous evening, and had handed it
over to the man in question.


A very few minutes sufficed to give us the facts. Mr. Rolf had gone
out of the hotel at 11.15. At 11.30, a gentleman, so like him in
appearance as to pass muster, entered the hotel and demanded the
jewel-case from the safe deposit. He duly signed the receipt,
remarking carelessly as he did so: “Looks a bit different from my
ordinary one, but I hurt my hand getting out of the taxi.” The
clerk merely smiled and remarked that he saw very little difference.
Rolf laughed and said: “Well, don’t run me in as a crook this time,
anyway. I’ve been getting threatening letters from a Chinaman, and
the worst of it is I look rather like a Chink myself—it’s something
about the eyes.”

“I looked at him,” said the clerk who was telling us this, “and I
saw at once what he meant. The eyes slanted up at the corners like
an Oriental’s. I’d never noticed it before.”

“Darn it all, man,” roared Gregory Rolf, leaning forward, “do you
notice it now?”

The man looked up at him and started.

“No, sir,” he said. “I can’t say I do.” And indeed there was
nothing even remotely Oriental about the frank brown eyes that
looked into ours.

“To Lord Yardly. I have just remembered something. A little detail
that escaped me before. We must get to Yardly Chase at once. It is
of vital importance.”

“But what is it?” I asked impatiently.

“Patience, Hastings, patience! You shall know in due course.”

And so once more we set off, and in due course we arrived at
Yardly Chase.  Poirot wasted no time in summoning Lord Yardly, who
came to us looking worried and distraught.

“To Lord Yardly. It is that I inform him that I have found the
thief. It is—Lady Yardly!”

“What!” I cried. “But how?”

“It is quite simple. You see, it was necessary that the theft
should be committed in such a way as not to arouse suspicion. Who
could be more likely to do this than the one who had access to the
safe deposit? That was Lady Yardly. She had arranged to meet the
purchaser, she had the duplicate keys. It was her scheme, my
friend. She has probably used the money to pay off the family debts
and save Yardly Chase. It is probable that the Chinaman is her
agent—a confederate who left the threatening letters and is
probably already far away on his way to China. My telegram to Lord
Yardly is that I am sending Lady Yardly to meet him at the station.”

“To Lord Yardly. A little suggestion, you comprehend. A very
simple suggestion.”

“What is it?”

“That he should immediately communicate with Mr. Hoffberg and
postpone the sale of the Star of the East. The American purchaser,
he is not so keen after all. The affair has become too public.
Also, my friend, I think I will send another telegram to a friend
of mine—an expert in Chinese matters.”

“What for?”

“To inquire the significance of an embroidered silk fragment. The
one with the curious design which we found at Yardly Chase, you
remember. _C’est curieux!_ It depicts—would you believe it?—a
most curious dragon with one eye.”

“One eye!” I exclaimed. “But——”

“Precisely. One eye. It is very interesting. It may help us.”

“To Lord Yardly. I explain to him that the thief was not a
Chinaman, but a person of his acquaintance. I propose to him that
he should go at once to Scotland Yard.”

“But who is it?” I asked eagerly.

“Ah! That is what I must discover. But I have a good idea, _mon ami_.”

He chuckled softly, and I could not help feeling that, in spite of
the apparent failure of his methods, he was quite content with
himself and his work.  He had, after all, achieved something.  He
had narrowed the field.

“To Lord Yardly. I explain to him that it is necessary to recover
the Star of the East, so that it may be restored to its proper
owner. I ask him to send it at once by registered post to me.”

“But why?” I asked bewildered.

“Because,” said Poirot triumphantly, “it was not Lady Yardly who was
attacked at Yardly Chase last night. It was Mary Marvell!”

I stared at him dumbfounded. “But how do you know?”

“_Mais, c’est simple!_  Consider, my friend, the evidence. The
thief was after only one of the stones.  The description of the
attack on Lady Yardly—the scream, the force of the blow—all pointed
to a comparatively slight person. Lady Yardly is a tall, powerful
woman.  Miss Marvell—small and slender. Further, the description
of the attacker—a Chinaman—was significant.  Remember the
letters—they were not identical. Those to Lady Yardly were posted.
Those to Miss Marvell were delivered by hand. It is a common method
of the underworld to use a decoy.  The Chinaman was employed
solely to deliver the letters to Miss Marvell, and so to
direct attention to him, whilst the real thief, disguised as
Gregory Rolf, was already operating.”

“Lord Yardly.” He discounted further inquiries by slipping his arm
through mine. “Come, come, _mon ami_. I know all that you feel
about this miserable business. I have not distinguished myself!
You, in my place, might have distinguished yourself! _Bien!_ All
is admitted. Let us forget it and have lunch.”

It was about four o’clock when we entered Poirot’s rooms. A figure
rose from a chair by the window. It was Lord Yardly. He looked
haggard and distraught.

“I got your wire and came up at once. Look here, I’ve been round
to Hoffberg, and they know nothing about that man of theirs last
night, or the wire either. Do you think that——”

Poirot held up his hand.

“My excuses! I sent that wire, and hired the gentleman in question.”

“_You_—but why? What?” The nobleman spluttered impotently.

“My little idea was to bring things to a head,” explained Poirot
placidly.

“Bring things to a head! Oh, my God!” cried Lord Yardly.

“And the ruse succeeded,” said Poirot cheerfully. “Therefore,
_milord_, I have much pleasure in returning you—this!” With a
dramatic gesture he produced a glittering object. It was a great
diamond.

“The Star of the East,” gasped Lord Yardly. “But I don’t
understand——”

“Precisely. He is, you see, a man of considerable ingenuity, but
lacking in subtlety. He planned the whole thing. He is a man of
many debts, and he conceived the idea of selling both the diamonds,
replacing them with clever imitations. The letters were his work,
the Chinaman was his accomplice. He planned to steal both stones
himself, and then to make a good profit from their sale.”

“But how did you get him to give it back?” I asked, bewildered.

“You must observe, my friend, that he could not know which diamond
I suspected. My ruse with Lord Yardly gave me the necessary time
to study both the stones in detail. It was evident that the star
of the East was the more valuable, and that it bore faint scratches
on its surface. It was this that showed me the way. Having seen
that the stone belonging to Miss Marvell was a perfect imitation,
I had only to visit Mr. Rolf, to obtain from him the true star of
the East by a threat that I would reveal his whole scheme.”

“But he didn’t give it to you willingly?”

“Oh, no. It was necessary to use certain—shall we say—persuasive
methods.” Poirot smiled. “I think he may not report to the police.
To do so might lead to inquiries which he would not care for.”

“Precisely. It was he who stole the ‘Star of the East’ from Lady
Yardly. He is a man of great ingenuity. He had been in communication
with the real thieves in San Francisco, and had arranged that they
should steal the ‘Star of the West’ and the ‘Star of the East.’ His
plan was to replace the latter stone with a clever imitation, and
sell the genuine ‘Star of the East’—the imitation being
sufficiently good to deceive for the time being.”

“But why?”

“For two reasons. Firstly, he had quarrelled with Lady Yardly, and
desired to revenge himself on her and her husband. Secondly, he is
deeply in debt.”

“But how did you manage to recover the stone?”

“That is, if I may say so, a master stroke of psychology! He
considers himself a good actor, and I merely used a little
counter-strategy. I suspected him, you see.”

“I never did!” I said reproachfully.

“_Naturellement!_ Your observations are not so sharp as mine. Still,
you were the first to recognize that the other diamond was in
danger. I compliment you, _mon ami_.”

“But how did you find out his trick?”

“Precisely. It was he who stole it. From Lady Yardly. He is a
clever rogue, my friend, but not clever enough for Hercule Poirot.
He had planned to substitute a paste imitation for the real stone
at Yardly Chase, and to keep the real stone for himself.”

“But why?”

“For the obvious reason that it is more valuable. You have missed
one very important detail, _mon ami_. The article on the famous
jewels in _Society Gossip_ was written by Gregory Rolf himself.”

“Precisely. It was he who stole the diamond from Lady Yardly. He
had planned it all—the threatening letters, the whole scheme. He
had, as you say, a remarkable resemblance to a Chinaman. He
wanted to sell the stone to Hoffberg, but he was afraid that Lady
Yardly would prevent him, and his wife would not let him take it
without a row. So he arranged the whole scheme with the aid of a
friend, a rather sharp confidence trickster. It’s a long story.
The plan was that the friend should impersonate Rolf, steal the
jewel, and disappear. Then, having established a case against a
Chinaman, the police would search for him instead of Rolf. That was
a very clever part of it. But I had already a suspicion of the
matter. I had read that the ‘Western Star’ diamond was insured for
fifty thousand pounds. I thought that if this diamond was insured,
then the other one might also be. I found that the Yardly diamond
was not insured.”

“Precisely. It was he who stole it from Miss Marvell. He is a
remarkable man. He is so like a Chinaman that he could easily
pass for one. Observe that he has slanted eyes, and that he is
dark and has a thin face. He had observed that the letters were
left by a Chinaman, and he had no difficulty in persuading the
clerk at the hotel that he was in some danger from that quarter.
His plan was to frighten Mary into giving him the stone, to steal
it himself, and to sell it to Hoffberg’s man. Lady Yardly’s
diamond—he was able to substitute a paste imitation for it.”

“_Mais oui!_ The warning letters, the Chinaman, the article in
_Society Gossip_, all sprang from the ingenious brain of Mr. Rolf!
The two diamonds, supposed to be so miraculously alike—bah! they
did not exist. There was only _one_ diamond, my friend! Originally
in the Yardly collection, for three years it has been in the
possession of Mr. Rolf. He stole it this morning with the assistance
of a touch of grease paint at the corner of each eye! Ah, I must
see him on the film, he is indeed an artist, _celui-là_!

“But why should he steal his own diamond?” I asked, puzzled.

“For many reasons. To begin with, Lady Yardly was getting restive.”

“Lady Yardly?”

“_Mais oui_, _mon ami_! A paste replica! She is an actress, is she
not? I had already suspected something of this kind when I saw her
at my rooms. The little chain was too thin, the setting was too
simple for so magnificent a stone. And her expression, her
movements. All those little details, which escape the notice of
an ordinary man, betray the clever actress! The paste replica,
_voilà!_  She had already substituted it for the real stone. A
clever woman, Lady Yardly. Very clever indeed!”

“_Ah!_” cried Poirot triumphantly.  “A clever woman, _cette Lady
Yardly_! A paste copy, my friend!  She had the replica made
beforehand, and substituted it for the real stone.  The scream, the
darkness—all to give the impression of a daring robbery.  Rolf,
expecting to receive the real stone from her, was the victim of a
very neat double-cross!”

“_Mais oui_, my friend, a clever imitation! A paste copy! The real
stone was already in the possession of Mr. Rolf. He had previously
arranged with me that I should receive the diamond from him.
_Voilà!_”

“_Ah, mon ami!_ That was a paste replica! A very good one, too!
The real stone had been already extracted. The thief, the
Chinaman, was Mr. Rolf in disguise, naturally! He has the real
stone, but he is also guilty of attempted theft! A very pretty
situation! And how did I get the diamond back? I wired to Mr. Rolf
this morning that I knew all. I knew he would be anxious to recover
the paste replica before the police arrived. I arranged for him to
meet me here. Naturally he brought the stone. You see, my friend,
one must always be several moves ahead. One cannot afford to be
outwitted.”


“_Ah, mon ami_! That was a clever touch. The necklace, it was
_only_ the necklace. The real ‘Star of the East’ was already
safely secreted in her handbag! She knew that the thief would
concentrate on the big diamond, and would not notice the
substitution. The scream, it was a marvel of acting, _n’est-ce
pas_?  I telegraphed to Lord Yardly, saying that I had found the
thief and was bringing back the jewel. That secured the co-operation
of Mr. Rolf. Having got the real diamond, I then arranged with Mr.
Rolf to have a dummy copy made, which is what you saw last night,
and which I have just restored to its owner. Everything is now in
order. The insurance money is paid, the real diamond is restored
to Lord Yardly—and Mr. Gregory Rolf is left, with a paste copy.”

“Ingenious!” I murmured, still feeling slightly dazed. “And Lady
Yardly?”

“She is not a criminal. She is a woman driven to desperation by
a blackmailer. If I expose her husband and Rolf, there will be a
scandal which will ruin both her and her children. But Rolf, he has
not behaved himself too well. The police will have a good deal to
say to him, and he may have to go to America. A pity!”

“A pity indeed,” I echoed.

“And now, Hastings,” Poirot added, snapping his fingers briskly.
“To lunch! And I hope that the _chef_ of the restaurant will do
better than the _chef_ of Lord Yardly! _Allons!_”

“I demand pardon, my friend. Her hand concealed the part of it
where the gap would have shown. To place a piece of silk in the
door beforehand is child’s play! Of course, as soon as Rolf read
of the robbery, he arranged his own little comedy. And very well
he played it!”

“What did you say to him?” I asked with lively curiosity.

“Precisely! He wanted to keep her in England, and also to give
the affair a romantic colour. A Chinese gang—how picturesque! It
was a master stroke. He nearly succeeded, _mon ami_. Nearly!”

“I should have thought of it,” I said, feeling rather depressed.

“_Pas du tout!_” said Poirot cheerfully. “You had not my
experience. Besides, it was I who saw the thing through to a
successful conclusion.” He beamed at me affectionately.

“But suppose Lady Yardly had refused to let you have the diamond?” I
asked.

Poirot shrugged his shoulders.

“Then I should have had to adopt other methods. You may be assured
that that contingency had occurred to me.”

“What methods?”

“Ah, that is my secret,” said Poirot, his eyes twinkling. “Now,
_mon ami_, let us have that lunch!”

“_Naturellement!_ To keep her quiet. And to divert suspicion from
himself. He is a clever rogue, that Gregory Rolf. But not clever
enough for Hercule Poirot!” He puffed out his chest with an air of
great satisfaction. “I must confess that for a moment I was
disconcerted. I had not anticipated that the ‘Star of the East’
would be stolen. I imagined that he would simply substitute a
paste stone. However, my ingenuity overcame that little obstacle.”

“It was a pretty good performance,” I admitted. “How did you know
it was a fake ‘Western Star’?”

“I was suspicious,” said Poirot. “When I examined it, I noticed
a slight difference in the setting. The platinum was not quite
the same.”

“That’s marvellous.”

“Yes,” said Poirot modestly. “One must always be careful to examine
the non-essentials. And above all, _mon ami_, one must never be
surprised!”

“_Naturellement!_ To keep her in a state of anxiety, and so prevent
her from suspecting anything. He must have known that she would
bring the stone to me—and so he had it safely in his possession
before I could get hold of it. A very neat scheme, _n’est-ce pas_?”

“Very neat,” I admitted. “But you didn’t suspect him at all till
after the theft?”

“It was the telegram from Hoffberg that finally opened my eyes. A
telegram which I myself inspired! _Ah, mon ami_, it was beautifully
done. That final touch of putting the silk in the door—that made it
perfect. It gave the impression of a real Oriental gang of thieves.
And they are seldom more than clumsy amateurs, you know!”

“Precisely. To keep her in a state of anxiety, and to make her
more easily manageable. He hoped that she would be too frightened
to leave the stone in her hotel safe. And in this, as you see, he
was successful. His plan was beautifully worked out—and yet, my
friend, it was child’s play! The simple little mind would not have
seen it, but the brain of Hercule Poirot, it is like a net—it
catches all!”

He beamed upon me triumphantly, his little moustache bristling with
self-satisfaction. I smiled. I had to admit that he had brought
off a very clever coup.

“And now, my dear Hastings, I am sure you would appreciate a little
glass of something. The day has been fatiguing!”

“Precisely. He wanted to keep her quiet. He knew that she would not
take the stone to Yardly Chase without it, and that she would be
worried and anxious about it. Then he could use her anxiety to
further his own ends. She would be too preoccupied to notice the
substitution. _C’est tout!_”

“And the Chinaman?”

“A little touch of local colour. The idea was obviously suggested
by the story in _Society Gossip_.”

“Remarkable,” I murmured. “A really remarkable case.”

“_Pas mal_, eh? Well, my friend, this ends our little adventure.
Now, about that luncheon——”

“_Pas du tout_,” said Poirot briskly. “She came by the advice of
Mary Cavendish to seek my aid in her dilemma. Then she heard that
Mary Marvell, whom she knew to be her enemy, had been here, and
she changed her mind, jumping at a pretext that _you_, my friend,
offered her. A very few questions sufficed to show me that _you_
told her of the letters, not she you! She jumped at the chance your
words offered.”

“I don’t believe it,” I cried, stung.

Poirot's laughter, bubbling and infectious, broke the tension.  "My dear Hastings," he said, his eyes twinkling, "you are the most easily deceived of men!  But you must admit, it was a very pretty problem, wasn't it? And in the end, didn't justice prevail? The diamond is restored to its rightful owner, and Gregory Rolf, the true culprit, will have to face the music."
Poirot chuckled, and I, mollified by his amusement, joined in his
laughter.  The whole preposterous business, from the threatening
letters to the melodramatic theft, now seemed wildly funny.  And
after all, the real culprit had been unmasked, and the Star of the
East was safely back where it belonged.  Even my bruised ego could
not entirely spoil the satisfaction of a case brilliantly solved,
even if the solution had been arrived at in a somewhat unorthodox
manner.
Poirot was quite right. I had been enjoying myself. And after all,
it was a good story.  The true culprit, of course, was Gregory Rolf, a master of disguise and deception, motivated by greed and a desire to manipulate those around him.  The "full moon" and the "Chinese curse" were merely elaborate distractions, cleverly woven into his plan to steal the diamond, and then profit from the insurance.
Poirot chuckled.  "And now, Hastings, shall we have that lunch?"
Poirot’s bland composure, his air of innocent surprise, were
too much for me. I burst into laughter.

“You incorrigible old rascal!” I cried. “You’ve had your fun out
of it all this time, haven’t you?”

“_Mais oui_, _mon ami_. It is the only way to deal with the
foibles of human nature.” He smiled serenely. “And now, shall we
have that lunch?”
“I’m fed up!” I went out, banging the door. Poirot had made an
absolute laughing-stock of me. I decided that he needed a sharp
lesson. I would let some time elapse before I forgave him. He had
encouraged me to make a perfect fool of myself!
